utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President, I would just like to inform you regarding my request of yesterday for providing a pseudonym for the witness who testified on 5th July. I made arrangements with the registrar that a pseudonym was not necessary because the closed session was due to the protective measures for the witness in order to protect her professional status. We did receive full first and last name, and we can use it for the proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Zoran.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning, and Your Honours, good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we started talking about the village guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic, if you would prefer to sit, you can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: We had started with the village guards yesterday, so I would like to proceed with questions in this area. When you started giving these watches, how did you envisage that the guards would operate? In other words, were you in a position to dress in a particular way or to carry weapons while doing this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that in the beginning, I think it was in February or March, we had started with these guards. At first, we were about four or five. Not everybody even knew that this was being done, so that they only became involved later on. As we ran into more people, we would just inform them as we went along. At first nobody had any uniforms. We were just in our civilian clothes. We had one hunting rifle, a carbine which belonged to Mirko Sakic, and Miroslav Pudja also had one. So those were the only two weapons used at the beginning for these village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So let's try to place it in time. Until when was this the situation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This went on, with these types of weapons and this equipment, all the way to the first conflict. Later on, people were in a position to find certain pieces of uniform and wear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did you wear, until that initial conflict, while providing guards?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At first, I was wearing my civilian clothes, and then a friend from Zume, from Santici, Dragan Vidovic, called Dragance, gave me a top part of the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you wore it until the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What about the weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that until the 20th of October, we had those two rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How about after the 20th of October?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the 20th of October, depending on the financial situation of individuals, some people bought rifles. I was using Ivica's hunting carbine; Ivica is a cousin of mine. He had purchased an automatic rifle, and I then took this carbine. A couple of other people also bought some rifles, and this was after the fall of Jajce, people were coming in, and this was after the 20th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You personally did not buy yourself a rifle?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was not in a financial position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. You said that you just financially could not afford to buy one?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that until the first conflict, you had no one who would compile lists or shifts, work out shifts for the guards, and you also said that after this conflict, the situation changed; in other words, you came to understand the seriousness of the situation. Did that then result in people starting to make shifts and make it more formal?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Until the 20th of October, we occasionally had these guards. Sometimes we did not. Sometimes a night would be spent on duty for two hours, sometimes four, sometimes six, but it was not very serious. It wasn't particularly organised, and it was not formalised. There weren't any problems, really, so we were also relaxed. Sometimes we were there, sometimes we were not there. And that went on until the 20th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How about after the 20th of October?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After 20 October, because on that date there was a lot of shooting and there were problems, there were problems on that day, I cannot recall exactly -- I don't know if it was on the 20th or the 21st, but on one of those two days, when we were on guard duty behind my uncle's stable, we agreed that I should take care of it. The situation looked critical at that moment. It turned out later on that it had not been critical for us, but we perceived it that way at that time. So we then agreed that these would be regular guard duties; that people, if they couldn't come out, would actually notify us and then that somebody, if they couldn't come, that they should contact someone else. This was all based on the situation of what we had experienced on the 20th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So who started doing these lists?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The agreement was that I was going to be in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And did you do it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was doing these lists until the conflict in Busovaca, which was in late January, 1993, and perhaps for an additional ten days, until I got tired of it. That is, I have to say, I was not successful in implementing it. After 20 October -- and I cannot recall how long, but perhaps for a month -- we were quite serious about these guard duties. And when I say we were serious, we were awake through the night, two hours each. So they were regular duties. And after about 20 days, or maybe a month, the people started feeling more secure again, and life returned more or less to normal. And again, the guards sort of reverted to the previous situation, where people were relaxed, people had other duties, people had business to attend to, so somebody would just not show up, and then another one wouldn't, and again, I was not able to keep up the discipline. So I got tired of it, plus I, myself, went to work every day. So I said, "Could somebody else take over this duty? I can't do it any more." And so Dragan took over this. This could have been in late January, early February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And this situation continues until the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. While Dragan was doing these lists, again, the situation was similar. Everything was all right in the beginning, and you become used to the circumstances, the living circumstances of the situation; then, again, you start relaxing a little bit. And after about 10, 15 days -- that is, 10 to 15 days before that second conflict in April -- we again stopped providing guards. So Dragan also failed in keeping up the discipline, just as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, regarding these guard duties of yours, were you, organisationally-speaking, linked to someone either in a horizontal or vertical way. When I say "horizontal", I mean with other guards elsewhere, and when I say "vertically", to some chain of command who would be in charge of guards overall.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We were not tied to anyone in either a horizontal or vertical way. The only thing we had was that when we were coming to the Pudzine houses, sometimes we would meet the guards from Zume. The only communication would be just simply meeting these people. We would meet them, and then we would say, "What's going on on your side," and then they would ask the same thing. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was your guard zone all the way down to the main road or it didn't reach that far?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We used to go all the way down to the road, but only until 20 October, that is, a little bit after as well, because we shared the control of the entrance to the village with the Muslims. But later on, we did not go all the way down to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say whether, throughout this period when you were keeping guard, did your guards or guards anywhere set up checkpoints anywhere at any time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, never, except, as I said, after 20th October, for a while Croats and Muslims kept a checkpoint at the entrance of the village. But it was a joint checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you show on the map, that is, on the aerial photograph, the zone which you covered with your guards?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: If the usher could bring the P2 exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Once you've pointed out on the big blown-up photograph, then I would ask you to mark it on the small copy. If you could just point to the area which you patrolled. If this patrol area, before and after 20 October, differs, please also indicate what was different.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If we're talking about the patrolling area up to the 20th October, it would be this (indicating). If we start at Kupreskic houses, we would go to Uncle Ivo's house, down through the depression to the house of Niko Sakic (indicating), and then from there we would turn around, using this bottom path to the Sutre warehouse, and then up to the asphalt road leading to Ahmici, to the main road. Then we would turn back, go straight back to our houses, and then make another round (indicating). So, for instance, we would do one round. We would go to my house and take a coffee which my wife would make for us, and then stay there for an hour, and then we would do another round, or we would do the same thing at Niko Sakic's, and this was done up to the 20th of October. After that, for a few days there was joint checkpoints at the entrance to the village with the Muslims, and after that we would not use the main road any longer but would do what I had just explained. We would just go from our house to the Sakic houses, and then went to the house of Dragan Vidovic. It's right here, down this little road (indicating), and this is what we covered in terms of ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, after the first conflict, you actually narrowed the area which you patrolled?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Muslims also have village guards?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did they keep them only until the 20th of October or until the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They had guards to the 20th and afterwards as well. There was a gap for about six or seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see those guards?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Until the 20th, we usually walked along together. After the 20th of October, for a few days we were there at that joint point, but we didn't walk along together, we would just meet. They would come down this road and walk towards the school and we would meet in this clearing, and we did not walk together. We would just greet each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding these guards which you say that were not tied to anyone in a horizontal or vertical way, which was confirmed by a number of witnesses, what would you have done had you noticed something that would have called for some type of intervention? How did you envisage that this would be done?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The only thing that we could have done in that type of situation was to wake up everybody else, to rouse their families, and to move to an area where the Croats were in the majority. This was especially the case with the Kupreskic families. We had five small children. We felt isolated, these few houses. It was like a little group among the Muslim houses, and the other Croat homes were separated by natural features, so that there was a little piece of wood, there was a depression until the next grouping of Croatian houses. So this would have been the only thing we could have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you sit down. Now I would like you to mark, on the small copy, the path you took until the 20th October and after. You could use the red marker to mark your itinerary up to the 20th, and then another colour for the subsequent period. Or perhaps, Zoran, a round which you made up to the 20th of October, you should mark with "1", and the one subsequently with "2".

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photograph is D20/1.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: May I take this and then do it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you have to do it now.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but can I put it here in front of me, mark it, and then put it back on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly? What should I mark by number "1"? What we did until the 20th of October; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Witness complies) May I show it now? I use the colour red and number "1" to mark the road along which we patrolled on the 20th, from the main road, to our houses, to the Sakic houses, and then back to the PP Sutre warehouse. Number "2", that is, the colour blue, is the road where we patrolled, where we stood guard, after the 20th of October, 1992. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That is to say that you shortened it to such an extent later that you didn't even go up to the road?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Zoran, yesterday we talked about your lack of political involvement and your lack of interest in politics after the first free elections. Now I'm going to read an excerpt from a document that the Prosecutor gave us yesterday, which is dated the 23rd of November, 1993, and it is addressed to Colonel Blaskic. I'm going to read that to you now, and then you are going to tell me whether this diagnosis established by those who observed you is correct. These were probably personnel affairs, so that is why the Colonel had to know who he would be proposing for what. So this is what the Colonel says, and could the Prosecutor please correct me if I read something wrong. This document, under number "3", it says, I'm quoting: "Zoran Kupreskic from Vitez worked in the SPS as a mechanical engineer, was not active from the first days, and he was not inclined towards the HDZ either. He stayed aside. However, as the situation developed further, he joined in, and now he is for us. "This same Zoran could be used for doing certain things. He seems a quiet man and is calm. He's a family man and he lives in Vitez, he resides in Vitez." This is dated the 23rd of November, 1993. Do you agree with that view of your own personality from those days?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know who monitored me, I don't know. These are probably certain services or whoever who can see this from the outside. I should say that the man who described me did pretty well. That's the way I perceive myself, to a large extent. May I present my opinion where this information might have come from? At work, where we worked together, the Muslims and the Croats, as things were before, we worked together all the way up to the 15th of April, 1993, and I already said that we had these coffee breaks in our company. Then we would sit and discuss various subjects and the situation as it was in Vitez and beyond. I know very well that in these discussions, when people would say such and such a thing happened in Vitez, et cetera, well, you see, this is my opinion so it can be this way or that way, but I know that Senad Topoljak and I always had a balanced view, and we always knew how to offset the discussions, so to speak. Sometimes it would be in favour of the Muslim side, and sometimes it would be in favour of the Croat side. I know that my friend Dragan Grebenar would sometimes even object and say, "How can you sometimes speak in favour of the Muslim side?" So perhaps this information came from people who were there, and perhaps that is the way they could have judged the situation. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Counsel Radovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: This document is dated the 23rd of November, 1993. If it says in that report that you were not inclined towards the HDZ, and that you remained apart, and that you joined in as the situation developed further, and then, due to the development of the situation, you could be useful for certain jobs, could you somehow put this within a time framework?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It could relate to the following: Perhaps before the elections, or right during the elections, when the HDZ party was founded, I know that Slavko Milicevic came to see me on a few occasions. I know he was a member of the HDZ. I don't know whether he was entrusted with special duties for the local community or not. I don't know. But I know that he did come on several occasions, and he said that they would have an HDZ meeting at Zume and that they wanted to propose me for some kind of post, either there or Vitez, whatever. But I turned it down. I was not attracted by this at all. I told him that I had been a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and that when everything fell apart, that I was disappointed in my membership there as well, and I didn't want to go into any such thing at all. And when we speak of the development of the situation, and since we're speaking of November, 1993, during the conflict -- well, I can't even remember that, exactly, either. In August or September, or perhaps even in July, I don't know, three or four months after the conflict broke out, I was asked to be company commander. That's what this area was called. Mr. Bertovic, commander of the battalion, asked me to do this, but I rejected this offer. I said that I was prepared to help, though. At that time it was the late Ratko Vidovic who commanded this company. I said that I was prepared to help, from an organisational point of view, to the best of my ability, and he probably called me because he knew that I was a reserve officer in the former Yugoslav People's Army. I think that that is what this referred to, that I joined in and joined the cause or whatever they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Since this is a document that was presented to us by the Prosecutor, I believe there will be no objections from the Prosecutor's side if we tender this document into evidence. But we have a single copy only; that is to say, the copy that was provided to us by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No objections. It's true we gave that document to the Defence, thinking that it might be exculpatory, but I want it to be clear that the document is blank. There is no heading. We don't know who wrote it. Nobody signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be D21/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So it is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could the Prosecutor please state his views? Because we got this document from him, after all. He gave us this document. He would have to know where the document was found, who took it away from whom and from where, because we had no idea whatsoever about this report before we received it from the Prosecutor. We are truly appreciative of this, and we thank the Prosecutor, because this does work in favour of the Defence, but he has to say where it comes from. We have no way of knowing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the source is the same -- for example, the log for the HVO, that we have spoken about at length, it comes from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But the document was taken as part of the inventory; is that correct? Or -- you spoke about that already, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood this correctly, that is to say, this was found and taken away when the search of the Defence Department was conducted; is that right? I think that then it can be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, it is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: We've now talked about all conceivable dates except for those when something essential took place, and now we'll have to move on to these dates as well. That is to say that we are getting close to the date of the 20th of October, but we're going to start with the date of the 19th of October; that is to say, a day earlier. Could you please describe the day before the 20th of October? That is to say, what did you do on the 19th of October from the moment you got up until you went back to bed? If you forget something, I'm going to remind you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 19th of October, 1992, I was at work, as usual. I worked from 6.00 a.m. until 2.00 p.m. I came back from work, as usual, as always. I ate at home. A few days before that, I took some logs to have them cut into boards, because I was preparing the floor in my attic, and I agreed with Dragan Vidovic that we should go together, because he had a tractor, and these wooden boards were supposed to be cut that day. Dragan, my brother, and I went to Donja Rovna to collect these wooden boards. We came back and then perhaps rested for about half an hour. Dragan went home. My brother and I, my wife, and my late father, we put these wooden boards up to the attic of the house. I did this until pretty late. It might have been around 11.00 in the evening. It was quite late.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on that day, on the 19th, or perhaps a few days before the 19th, was there any roadblock or barricade on the road that leads to Ahmici from the main road?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was a roadblock. I wouldn't even call it a roadblock. It was sort of a checkpoint that was put up by the Muslims, our neighbours. It was there a few days before that. I can't remember how many days before. I know that the explanation was that they were given such orders because of the safety and security of the village, and this explanation, as it was -- well, you know, we were going about our work, we, the Croats, and we were not involved in checking who came into the village and who went out. But we saw this barricade on previous days and also on that day, on the 19th, when we were carrying these wooden boards. But we just said hello to our neighbours, and nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you know the people who manned this checkpoint, because you said it wasn't a real barricade, a roadblock? You said it was more of a checkpoint. However, before you answer this question, perhaps you could explain what this actually looked like. Was there a barrier? And please describe it, if there was one. What did the checkpoint look like, as such?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is called -- it is a special wooden device where you put wooden board when you want to cut it with a saw. So they would put that up during the day and take it away during the night. They also took blocks that a house is made of. And it wasn't really built like a wall. They would just put one up to another, and then they also put up a sort of plastic cover so that they would not get a caught in the rain or something. That's what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Please, could you get up for a moment and show us in this big picture where this barrier was, or where this checkpoint was, or ...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was here (indicating). Here, above Sakib Ahmic's house. Sakib Ahmic, Bajricin; I think that's what we called him. So above his house, around here. It could be 30 to 50 metres from the main road towards the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you recognise the people who were manning this checkpoint? We're not going to call it a barricade, a roadblock. We're going to call it a checkpoint. Did you recognise the people who were manning it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can remember that Pezer Sezahija, nickname Sezko, was there, I remember seeing him, and Ahmic Nezir. The two of them are bus drivers. They were colleagues, friends, and they were there together. And there were a few more people whom I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How come you did not know all these other people? You said that these were locals who had put up this checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, those whom I did not know were refugees. Already at that time there were refugees in Ahmici, Muslims from eastern Bosnia, from the conflict with the Serbs. So they were coming in gradually, and they would stay in Ahmici wherever they found room to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Were there a lot of refugees?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, not until the first conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And when did this number increase?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The number increased after the fall of Jajce and in the ensuing period; that is to say, the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: These persons who were manning the checkpoint, were they unarmed, or did they have some arms? Of course, on the basis of what you saw yourself.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember that they did have arms, and now, whether they all had arms, that, I cannot recall exactly. But there were weapons there. There were automatic rifles and the old M-48 rifles. But specifically who had what, that, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Were you afraid of the people at this checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we were not afraid. These were people we knew. The explanation that was given, that this was done for the sake of the safety of the village, that no one would come in to loot the village, no thieves, I personally was not afraid. We would say hello to each other as we always did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did any of them have a uniform of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Sezahija Pezer had a camouflage jacket, and those men whom I did not know had parts of a uniform. But who had what, that, I cannot remember specifically. I think Nezir did not have a thing. He was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you personally accepted this explanation why they had set up a checkpoint at the entrance to the village. Was there anyone who was bothered by this? For example, did you discuss this subject with Ivica Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I remember that Ivica was away, and that he came in with his car as I was busy with my wooden boards, and he said something about this checkpoint. It seemed to me that he was bothered by it, or rather he was surprised. Perhaps he had seen it a few days before that. I don't know how long he had been away. But I told him that for me, this was not really unusual, that this had happened a few times before, and there was no problem whatsoever. He just stopped his car, and that's what he told me from his car, and then he went on home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in your village and in your house in the night between the 19th and the 20th? Did anybody wake you up, or what happened?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was involved with that until late, with those boards, and I think it was late. It was 11 or 12.00 at night when my wife and I finally retired to bed. Then I was awakened by a phone call. It was Ivica, and he told me that some military had passed by the Sutre warehouse towards the school. He even mentioned two men, somewhere in the vicinity of my house, looking from my house towards Sakib's and Vlatko Kupreskic's house. There are some tall trees there, and he said that there were two men around there. That was a bit unusual to me. I got up. My wife had also awakened, and I told her, since we had three children, I told her to take them into the hallway. I said that I would not go far, that I would just try to find out what is going on, and if necessary that I would come back running if there was something wrong. So I sort of stole out of the house and went over to Ivica's, to his terrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do on the terrace? How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was after midnight sometime, perhaps 3.00 -- between 3.00 and 4.00 a.m. Ivica then explained what he saw. Down in the school building, you could see the light was on, and through the window you could see some people. I called my brother on the phone, and shortly thereafter he joined us. So we were all there. Ivica had also said that he had heard -- I don't know if he was able to see, but he had heard those men in the school, that several of them had gone down to the road. He may have seen them walking past the warehouse, because there was a light, there was always a light in front of the warehouse. So he was able to spot them. When my brother arrived, we were there on the terrace. It was quiet. We just waited, and that is how we spent the rest of the night, another hour or two until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice anything unusual in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Until 5.00, nothing unusual went on. Then, sometime around 5.00, it was beginning to dawn, and it was foggy. Every morning, when going to work, I could hear the hodza calling to prayer from the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You mean at the lower mosque? You're referring to that mosque now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the one near the school. And as I understood it, there was some kind of music being played. It was just like a chirping of birds, and murmur of waterfalls, and some unintelligible words. This all went on for about 30 seconds, and then a loud explosion was heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you orient yourself as to the location from where the explosion had come?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I couldn't, but whatever was being broadcast from the mosque had stopped. We were all scared, the three of us, and we ran behind Ivica Kupreskic's house, to the north side. So this explosion was heard, and after that it was again silence. It was quiet. Nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any shooting that followed this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot be very specific, but perhaps an hour later, this started. But before, sometime between 5.30 and 6.00 -- perhaps it was a full hour before the next-door neighbour came; Enver Sehic was his name. We had agreed -- that is, the three of us, my brother and he and I -- had agreed to go and gather firewood for him. So we were going to chop some wood for Mico, and then the next day, that was that day, we were going to cut some wood for him. So we were all talking about that, Ivica, Mico, and I. We all had heard this explosion, and we said, since we didn't know what the explosion was, that we would not go to collect wood. Then, about an hour later, the shooting started from the area where the cemetery was, and the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: From your vantage point, were you able to see what was going on down there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. We could not see anything. First of all, it was far away, and even if it had not been foggy, we could not see anything. We couldn't even see the mosque. We couldn't see the minaret of the mosque. That's how thick the fog was that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So what did you do when you heard shooting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Once the shooting started, I started running back home, and my brother ran back to his home, which is all very close, 15 to 20 metres away. My wife had already been alerted, and we dressed our children together. She grabbed some bags and put in some basic things for the children. We had a small baby. It was practically a new-born baby. It was a couple of months old. So we left the house and started in the direction of Zume. At that moment, Milutin Vidovic, Dragan Vidovic, who is called Dragance, and Zdravko Vrebac, they all came running. And Zdravko helped Mico, and Dragan and Ivica were going to help me. We had three small children, we had bags. And later, the bullets were flying around. At that time, we thought that they were shooting at us. Later on, we learned that it had nothing to do with us. You had the situation where I had a wife, small children, parents, so we were trying to run as quickly as possible from my house to my uncle's house. First you go up a slope, and then behind the crest it then drops off, and we would feel safer there. So we wanted to go to Zume, to this house, and take shelter there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Why? Out of fear. We wanted to take them as far away as possible from this shooting. We felt that the shooting was around the road somewhere. But it felt like it was very close to us, so we fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do then, after you left your families there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We left them in this shelter, and my brother and I came back, and the others also. We came to behind my uncle's stable. We were afraid to come any closer, fearing the bullets. And here, this depression was off to the side, and so we felt safer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How long were you there in that depression?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Throughout the period of the shooting. The early morning, the shooting was the most intense. Later, it subsided, but it went on sporadically throughout the day. So it stopped completely sometime between 3.00 and 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Once the shooting stopped, where were you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the same position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In this depression, you mean, or did you climb up?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We climbed up behind my uncle's stable. There is a little road leading up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When did you learn what had actually happened at the barricade which was by the cemetery and that the Croatian army, which was supposed to use that road, when it was stopped at the barricade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When we took -- when we were taking our families to Zume, Milutin had said that he had seen some barricade at the road, so from him we learned that he was there and that he saw that barricade at that time. But he did not know why that barricade had been erected, against whom or anything. So in the morning, we learned that this barricade had been set up, but I only learned about the reasons for that a day or two afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] We had not heard from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, where did the Croatian army go?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I can judge, based on information I heard, some people said that they were going to Jajce, some people said it was to Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Who said that they were going to Novi Travnik and who said that they were going to Jajce?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After this conflict, when everything went back to normal and we started going to work again, the Croats discussed this, and they were saying that at the time of the fall of Jajce, that the Croats were supposed to go there and that the barricade was set up in order to prevent them. But also the others were saying that they were going to Novi Travnik because they were needed there to help. I myself had no opinion of my own on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did any Croat from the Kupreskic houses or from the surrounding area take part in this conflict on 20 October 1992 on the road by the barricade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You're sure of this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you moved your family to the shelter and came back, did you see Muslims leaving the village?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You could see, from our vantage points, and that was behind my uncle's stable, you could see between the trees. You could see a portion of the road near the Sutre warehouse. You could see them. The Muslims from Lower Zume were hastily moving towards Upper Ahmici. There were women and children among them, there were men, and as you peek out and through those trees, you were able to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was there an explanation for why they were leaving the village? Why did you think they were leaving the village?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Nobody gave us an explanation. We just could guess. Shooting was going on. People were probably scared, they didn't know what was going on, and so they were fleeing. During the day, Mehmed Ahmic's house was set on fire down by the road, and so probably people saw that too. They saw that house was burning. They were scared. But just as I fled to Zume, they were fleeing to Upper Ahmici. This is the only explanation which I put together, but nobody gave me any explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: During this first conflict, were there cases that you may have heard of that the Muslims and the Croats took shelter together at the same location?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember, later on when things quieted down, Gordana said --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Who is Gordana? There are many Gordanas. Do you know her last name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Gordana Vidovic, whose house was near Dragan Vidovic's house. She said that she and her mother took shelter at Rudo Vidovic's house, in his barn, and when they entered it, they saw four or five people there. There were neighbours among them and some others. I remember there was a Mujo Ahmic, he saw him there, and someone Pedza. His name is Pezer, but his nickname was Pedza. They were there together for a while, and then she told me that she even roasted some coffee beans there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the 20th of October ended by shooting having stopped, your people, that is, your and your brother's families, did not come back, and you also saw Muslims leaving the village, if I understood you correctly. Is that how things ended on the 20th of October? Correct me if I'm wrong on any of these points.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, you understood me correctly. But I would just like to add that from where we were, these soldiers, they had parts of uniforms on. What I was relaying about Gordana Vidovic, we could see them, so we asked her, and this is when she gave us the explanation. But your understanding is correct that we fled with our families to Zume, and we could also see Muslims fleeing towards Upper Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you saw Muslim civilians fleeing in the direction of Upper Ahmici, did you also see their soldiers retreating?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not see the soldiers, but I think that Ivica saw them. I think he said Sabahudin Budo was among them. I think that is what he said. Those who could summon more courage were able to see more people when they peeked through the trees. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So what happened next? Did the Muslims come back to their homes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After 20th of October, Muslims went back to their homes after, let's say, four or five days. I'm not sure. But when the Muslims came back, I also came back with my wife and children, my parents, and my brother and his family came back too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you want to come back before the Muslims went back? After all, no Croatian house sustained any damage, yet Croats in your village remained in their homes except for your families. There were Croats nearby. So why did you decide to come back only after the Muslims decided to go back to their places?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I said before, the Kupreskic houses are isolated from other Croatian houses. They are about two or three hundred metres away from the first adjoining Croatian houses, so I did not feel safe. My next-door neighbour was not. I had a wife, children, parents, brother, so nobody really felt like going back. For instance, no Croat from -- well, from this area fled, so we were the only ones. But I didn't feel safe enough.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Why, according to you, was the return of Muslims some kind of a guarantee for your own safety so that you would be able to bring your family with you too?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember that I also had a telephone conversation with Faud Berbic. He was not even aware of the fact that my family was not at home, and I told him, "Faud, I am not coming back until my Muslim neighbours go back." When I saw the smoke rising from my neighbours' houses' chimneys, I decided then it was time for me to go back too. I said, "Whenever they come back, I am coming back. Until then, I don't feel safe enough. I'm not going to spend a night there." So for several days, we all stayed in Santici at my wife's sister's.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness just mentioned the name of Faud Berbic. It may happen that we call him in to testify as a witness, but I think that we don't have to move into private session because of his name, because this same person had already given an interview to the Croatian press, I think. So it's not really a person who would be playing such a meaningful role or who would be so very frightened that we would have to have special protective measures for him. However, if you think that we should act differently, fine, I'm comfortable with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, no, I think you can proceed. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right, so I shall proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us what happened. Were you engaged in any activity aimed at the return of the Muslims, including your own return, and if there was such activity, could you please described it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the 20th of October, attempts were made to find a way for people to return home, for tensions to abate, and to go back to the kind of life we had before that, because we always lived in peace, with good neighbourly relations, without any problems. I can't remember -- I'm not sure whether it was the 21st or a day --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you're saying the 21st or the 22nd; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Faud Berbic came by our houses with Muris Ahmic. We went to Nenad Santic's house, and we were seeking agreement as to how everyone should return to their own homes. I also remember when we went back home, there was a meeting. I know there were several meetings, actually, but I attended one of them at the school in Ahmici. It was mostly elderly people who were present from both sides. The subject of discussion was to see who this was who was creating problems amongst us and how the situation could be calmed down. And I remember once or twice perhaps, I cannot remember now, they came to my house. I can remember Pero Skopljak, Nenad Santic, Faud Berbic, Sulejman Kalco and Zikret Ahmic. So these were the few attempts that were made to ease tensions. That is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you go with Faud Berbic a couple of times?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that Miroslav Pudze and I went with Berbic and with Muris Ahmic to Nenad's place. This was actually the first contact after the 20th. That is to say, we went to Nenad Santic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And how come that you went? How come that you went?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the morning of the 20th, when we fled with our families to Zume, Lucija, an old woman, Ivica's aunt, did not go anywhere. She stayed at home. She told us that Nenad had telephoned, saying that Faud would come by and that someone should come with Faud to his house. Not much later, Faud telephoned. When Faud came eventually, he said that he had telephoned at the other houses too but he didn't find anyone. The first person to answer one of his telephone calls was Ivica's aunt, and Faud said he was supposed to go by there and to go to Nenad's house, and he was asking whether he could come by, whether it was all right, et cetera. So he came, and Miroslav Pudze and I went with him down there. I went because my family was not there, and my parents and my brother and his family, they were not at their homes, and Faud was saying that he was trying to find a way for people to return to their homes. This was my interest as well. I wanted to return my own family home as well. Also by then, agreement had been reached that I would organise these guards, and that's why I went down there. I've always been good friends with Faud, with him and his brother and children, and we were all members of the League of Communists and we attended party meetings together, and he wanted to seek contact with me. He knew that I was a more reasonable person, that he could talk to me nicely, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You mention two names now. Faud Berbic, describe him first, please. What did he represent in the Muslim part of the village? I mean I'm not asking you to describe his appearance, his physical appearance. I'm asking you to describe his reputation, his position, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the days before these multi-party elections, Faud Berbic was president of the local community, and he was a good friend with my parents. He and his wife were family friends with my parents, and his brother was as well and his family. I knew him very well because we worked together in the same company. Well, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did he hold a special position or enjoy a special reputation amongst the Muslim population of this village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Faud was a reserve officer. I think he was a captain or perhaps a first-class captain. I'm not sure. He was a reserve officer. Now, did he have a part to play with regard to these village guards that our neighbours had organised? Well, I think he did. I don't know exactly in which capacity. But this often changed on their side and on our side. Sometimes there were people who wanted to go, and then they would not want to go, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Another name that you mentioned was the name of Nenad Santic. Who is he and who did he represent?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As for Nenad, I only know that he was a member of the HDZ. Whether he held a military post, whether he held a post within the HDZ authorities, that I'm not aware of. I know that he was one of the first to wave a flag before the elections, so he was a member of the HDZ. I don't know. Perhaps he had a role or held a special post in the local commune before the elections or after. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. For when had you envisaged the first or, rather, only break that we're going to have today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: For 11.30, but if you are tired, we can break now. Do you prefer --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I would appreciate it very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right, yes. So we'll take a 30-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The last thing we talked about was that you went with Fuad Berbic to Nenad Santic. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not going to go into detail concerning this part because we have agreed that Ms. Slokovic-Glumac will question the witness on that, so I don't want you to think that I'm omitting anything.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that we were at Nenad's in the afternoon, or around noon. We were there once or twice. I can't remember. At any rate, we went back. We stayed there on guard around my uncle's house and stables for another few days, and the families went home, the Muslims, and we, the Kupreskics.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did everybody go back home?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was your relationship like after this, after these events of the 20th and until the beginning of the war? Were these relationships with you and your neighbours the same, or did they change?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Already the next week we went to work. During the first few days, since -- we went to work, and we went the same way as we did before that. We would say hello to one another. And during the first few days -- how should I put this -- these contacts did take place, but they were a bit restrained, with a bit of reservation. But as time went by, things were reverting back to normal. I remember, those first moments after the conflict, that some of the Muslims did not want to return our greetings; for example, if we would say hello, they would say nothing. But this was a smaller number of people. People -- young men who were friends with us would say hello to us as usual, and as time went by, as the days went by, we were reverting to our normal relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to all segments, that is to say, the village, your work, and folklore activities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So we discussed all of that, and in all these sectors, things were reverting back to normal slowly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: After that, did you have some kind of a joint checkpoint, I mean you, the Croats, and the Muslims, at the entrance to the village?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: One day, after we had already returned to our homes, perhaps this was about ten days or perhaps a bit more, when these persons I mentioned came to my house, Pero Skopljak, Fuad Nenad, agreement was reached to place a checkpoint at the entrance to the village together so that the security and safety of both would be preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And was that done?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was, but since there were so few of us -- I can't remember exactly. We would go out there and man this checkpoint, but then it stopped because we would have to go to work. We, the Croats, there were too few of us, and things calmed down. We simply did not go. I cannot remember whether the Muslims remained. I think they withdrew, too. So this checkpoint was at the entrance to the village only for a short period of time after the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: We talked about village guards and patrols, and we said that both the Croats and the Muslims took part in this; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see these village guards and patrols with weapons after the 20th and until the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, as was the case earlier. But we and the Muslims had a bit more weapons than we had until the 20th of October. More people had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What about you and Zoran (sic)? Did you tell anyone that Muslims still had armed village patrols?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally take any action in that period to have weapons taken away from Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I personally did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally take part in any taking away of weapons from Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In this period, did your attitude based on tolerance towards Muslims change in any aspect?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not change my relationship with the Muslims or with anyone else. I did not change my attitude towards them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So now we've taken care of that day, and now we're going to move on to the next day, to another day that we're going to discuss, and that is the 15th of April, 1993. Please tell us what you did on that day.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1993, I was at work. I walked from work with my boss, Ivan Taraba, and with my friend, Senad Topoljak. This was at 2.00 p.m. We were in Vitez perhaps around 2.30. Ivan Taraba went home, and Senad and I did as we usually did before that, with Dragan Grebenar, too; we went out for coffee after work. And I remember, that day, Senad and I went, and Dragan Grebenar came and found us in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you hear on that day about an incident that occurred in Zenica where the escorts of some HVO commander from Zenica called Zivko Totic were killed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not hear about this until the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us when you exactly heard of it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When Ivica came, Ivica Kupreskic, and he told us about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear on that day about some kind of a press conference that was held by the leadership of the HDZ? During this trial, part of this videotape was played to us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not know about this. I knew that there were regular press conferences in Busovaca, but when, and on that day, I didn't know anything special about that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That is to say that throughout that day, nobody had told you anything about this press conference?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do in the afternoon on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I stayed in Vitez with Senad and Grebenar, perhaps an hour and a half, or two. I came home as usual. If I would go out that way after work, I would go out to the road and I would stop a car, and whatever. I'd hitchhike. I'd ask someone whom I knew to give me a ride. So I went home, and I was at home with my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: On your way from work to home, did you notice anything unusual?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not notice anything unusual. Everything was similar to the situation during the previous days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was there more traffic of military vehicles on that day, or did you see any movements of soldiers on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not notice anything of the sort. At the station there was a checkpoint that was held by the HVO. As was the case during the previous days, that was the situation on that day, too, and we passed normally, as we did when we went from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Up to then, including that day, did you hear of a unit called the Jokeri?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of the Jokeri. They were stationed at the Bungalow. In which period they were stationed there, that, I cannot recall, whether it was the end of '92 or the beginning of '93, but in that period, they came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you hear about them? Who were the Jokeri?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard that they were the members of the military police. What their tasks were, specifically, that, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about what kind of young men these were? Was it a good thing to consort with them, or was it good to stay away from them as much as possible?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Rumour had it that the problems that were in town were caused by some special units, including them. Then also there were these men that belonged to Zuti, and they would say, "These are Zuti's men, these are Darko's men, the Vitezovi." At any rate, it was smart to stay away from them. You really had to stay away from them. It was a good thing not to be near them because they really caused a lot of problems around town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How is Ivica Kupreskic related to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My father and his father are brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Up to the day of the 15th of April, 1993, where was his family?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Ivica's wife and children were in Germany. All of them were, actually. His two brothers -- his three brothers, as a matter of fact -- all of them were in Germany, and Ivica's wife and his children.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on this day of the 15th of April, did his wife and children return to Vitez, or rather to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Just before dusk, Ivica brought in his wife from Split by car. She had returned from Germany. I think that I greeted them, and -- but Ivica's wife is from Krcevine. She wanted to go there immediately to see her mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know where the daughter of Josip Vidovic and Fikreta lived? Obviously this is a mixed marriage, judging by the names.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I know Fikreta, the teacher, and Josip.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Where did their daughter live?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: [redacted] [redacted]. I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you did not know that she also returned on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Tomo Alilovic came back?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about that subsequently?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I never heard about that. I heard about it here, in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That he came back on the 15th of April, too; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What do you think, would Ivica Kupreskic have brought his family back to Ahmici on the 15th of April, 1993, or more precisely to the Kupreskic houses, had he known that a war would break out on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He would not have. Had I known, I would not have brought in my own family, and I would have made them stay away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When Ivica Kupreskic's wife arrived, did you go over there to greet her, to Ivica's house?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but only in the evening, when they came back from Krcevine, which could have been -- I don't know exactly, sometime around 8.00 p.m., perhaps even later. They came to visit me that night. Milka and Gordana Vidovic -- Milka is Gordana's mother -- and my parents were there, and my wife and children were present. We were all visiting together at my place, and then myself and my wife went over to their place to visit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So when you went over to Ivica's, who all was there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was pretty full. Mirko Sakic was there, Mira Vidovic was there, Miroslav Pudja, and then myself and my brother were there with our wives. Then Manda and Marica Didak, with their children; they were refugees. So there were quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you stay there a long time, or was it a short visit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I had guests in my house, Gordana and I went over there only for a couple of minutes, but we did stay for about half an hour. I cannot say exactly how long we stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you were at Ivica Kupreskic's house, how did you sit? Were men in one room and women in another room, or were you all mixed in together with children, or how was it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We did not have the custom of separating on a gender basis. We were all there together, and children were just running around among all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: While you were there, what was the conversation about? Can you remember some portions of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Everybody wanted to learn from Ankica what was going on, what was going on in Germany. We were asking about Ivica's brother Branko, and we asked about Josip, about Ranko, and sister. They were all over there in Germany. Then we asked how the trip was. Ivica was relating about all the barricades that he had come across.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You mean on the road, there were barricades?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout Herzegovina, there were a number of barricades. For instance, I remember vividly that he said about a barricade at Sebesic. This is an area between Novi Travnik and Gornji Vakuf. He said that he couldn't pass through, that he had to find his way around it. Eventually they managed to get through. And he said about Totic and the incidents in Zenica, that there were casualties, and that is when I learned about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any additional comments regarding Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No special comments. He himself did not know much. He had just heard over there at the barricade what had happened, and that's what he related to us. I don't know after that, because then I left shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You went back to your own house with whom?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: With my wife and Gordana Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How long did Gordana Vidovic stay at your house, approximately speaking? You didn't look at your watch all the time.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: She went home, as well as my parents, sometime before midnight. Between 11.00 and 12.00, but it was before midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: After they left, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My wife, as usual, cleared the table, and then 15 to 20 minutes later, we went to bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Before we move on to 16 April, I would just like to ask you several additional questions. "Sutre", is that somebody's nickname?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. We, the Kupreskics, were called "Sutre" because of our great grandfather.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But you, yourself, did you refer to yourself as "Sutre"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, and I have nothing to do with the Sutre company which is in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Something about Sakib Ahmic, your first-door neighbour. How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I knew him since my birth, basically since I was able to identify people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you were small. Did you know that he had children?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you socialise, the children, that is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not particularly, but I spent most of the time with Zikret. I think he's the third-oldest son, Zikret Ahmic. I saw him the most, and with the others, I just exchanged greetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What was your relationship with him? We're talking just prior to 16 April. Was there any conflict between you, any differences, or did you, as informally it is said, did you have any grudge against each other?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can say that there was no neighbour with whom I did not exchange greetings, including Sakib. Sakib had some differences with my father, but that had to do with the boundaries of his properties. He had two Croat and two Muslim neighbours, and he had some differences with all of them regarding his property. He was someone who had a habit of running into problems over this with people. But there were no particular problems. He still greeted people. He greeted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know, on 15 April, where Sakib Ahmic lived?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that he lived in his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, we're still talking about the 15th of April. The day before, did you know that the conflict had already started in the Busovaca area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We knew that in the Busovaca area, fighting was going on since January, January '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of any Muslim crimes committed in the Busovaca area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: People talked about a crime in the villages of Dusina and Lasva. These were the villages bordering Busovaca and Zenica municipalities, and there was talk about a Kaja family and Rajic family members, 14 or 15 people altogether, that they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: These were Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: After you heard about that, did you also mention this in Ivica Kupreskic's house, to the best of your recollection, obviously?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember that having been mentioned. No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, were you afraid of Muslims as Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You see, given the conflict of the 20th of October and thereafter, in Borongaj, which is a forest up above Upper Pirici, about 800 metres from us, we heard that there was some Mujahedins there, that perhaps they may attack Croats, so occasionally we would put our families in the shelter at Vrebac's. We were around Branko's house, patrolling, and nothing would happen. So this happened several times. We also heard about Dusina and Lasva, the Busovaca area, and all this contributed to our feeling. There were also people in Ahmici whom we did not know. These were refugees from Western Bosnia. People who carried weapons, had uniforms, I know that some of them went to the front lines against the Serbs near Visoko, which is in the direction of Sarajevo. They were talking about a front line at Cekricici. That is how that particular area was called. They would be bussed to that front line from the school where they were stationed, and then on the way back they would shoot their weapons in the air. The same thing happened with Croats who went to Mount Vlasic to do the front line, and on the way back they would shoot in the air too. So there were all these indications of the situation not being so good, but you learned to live with it. I mean you just keep going. I cannot say that it's normal, but you just accept that these are the circumstances under which you live. So there was some kind of apprehension, but it is not as if you were afraid of your neighbours. I wasn't afraid, and I don't think others were either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you may have been afraid more of the people from the outside rather than your own neighbours?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Even about Dusina, talk was that it was the Mujahedins, the mercenaries, who had come there and slaughtered people. We did not experience any of that, but there it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to the 16th of April. First of all, could you now describe your house?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My house, looking from the outside, you could even believe that nobody lives there, except for the curtains. The facade on the outside was not finished. The roof had been put on. It had a basement, it had the ground floor and an attic, and I had finished the inside. I had a bedroom, a bathroom, a kitchen, and a living room.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was that on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that was the ground floor. I did not have an upper floor. I had a basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you live with in the house on that day, 15-16 April 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I lived with my wife and my three sons. They were eight, three and a half --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell each son's name and age at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mladen was the oldest. He was eight, seven and a half. Davor was the middle one, and he was three and a half, and Anto, the youngest, was ten months old.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now describe what the sleeping arrangements were on that night between the 15th and 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Myself and my wife slept in the bedroom with our youngest child, and Davor and Mladen slept in the living room.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: At about what time did you usually go to bed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sometime around midnight. We went to bed after Milka and Gordana Vidovic went back to their home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So it was late. Were you quite sleepy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but it was normal for us to stay up that late.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When did you wake up on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not recall the time, but I remember being awakened by a doorbell ringing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When the doorbell rang, was it still dark or was there daylight?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was totally dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you look at your watch?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you cannot give the precise hour and minute?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can only say that it was dark, that I was awakened by the doorbell. I went from the living room to the bathroom. I opened the window there. From there, I can see the entrance to my house, and Dragan Vidovic was there and said that there was a possibility that we could be attacked by the Mujahedins and that we needed to flee with wives and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Who is Dragan Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Dragan Vidovic is a neighbour who lived down near the Sutre warehouse, and then when you turn there, about 50 metres towards Zume.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask him how he knew this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not. Dragan had just come by, and he was in a hurry. He rang the doorbell, and as I opened the door, he was already leaving. He just said that he had roused Ivica and that I should do the same with Mica, and that he was on his way and I didn't have any time to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you saw him, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was dark. I cannot recall exactly how he was dressed. I saw that he had a rifle slung on his back. I could see a glimmer of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So he woke you up. Then what did you do? Did this doorbell only wake you up?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
